item.title: Rosneft stretches refinery repairs from days to months as Ukraine strikes bite
item.description:
The main effect is on refined products rather than crude. Slower repairs mean Russian refining capacity stays offline for longer, keeping diesel and gasoil exports constrained just as the Northern Hemisphere heating season begins and middle distillate markets are already tight. That supports diesel crack spreads and refining margins elsewhere. When Russian refinery runs fall, more crude is typically freed up for export, which can partly offset the supply impact on crude markets. Even so, Brent near $113 is being driven far more by the risk of renewed US strikes on Iran than by Russia. For US consumers, the news makes a quick fall in diesel prices, now around $6.30 a gallon, even less likely before the midterm elections.

---

Earlier:

  • Trump invokes Defense Production Act for oil as pump prices bite 12 days before midterms

---

Rosneft has concluded that rebuilding refineries only to see them hit again is a losing game, which suggests Russia’s fuel export capacity may stay impaired for months, not weeks.

Summary:

  • Rosneft is deliberately slowing refinery repairs at most of its plants, stretching work that could take days into months, Bloomberg reported.
  • Refineries brought back online within weeks of attacks were struck again as repairs neared completion.
  • Rosneft officials have privately warned that the costs cannot be sustained, and that a few more months of war could cause severe, lasting damage to the business.
  • Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky ended a brief pause on refinery strikes last week, and Ukrainian drones hit Rosneft’s Ryazan refinery the same day.
  • Russia has restricted diesel exports for months because of refinery outages, and seaborne fuel exports fell sharply in early October.
  • The development casts doubt on how much diesel Russia can supply under the deal announced by President Trump.

Rosneft, Russia’s largest oil producer, is deliberately slowing repairs at most of its damaged refineries, stretching work that could be completed in days into months, according to Bloomberg. Repeated Ukrainian drone strikes have made the cycle of damage and reconstruction too expensive to sustain.

According to the report, refineries that Rosneft restarted within weeks of an attack were hit again as repairs neared completion, wiping out the investment. Company officials have privately warned that the costs cannot be sustained over the long term, and that a few more months of war could inflict catastrophic and lasting damage across the business.

The shift comes days after Kyiv resumed its campaign against Russian refining. President Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on October 11, and Ukraine held off from refinery strikes for three days. Zelensky ended that pause on October 15, telling the Financial Times that the restrictions on attacking refineries were over, after Russia kept up its strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Ukrainian drones set fire to Rosneft’s Ryazan refinery, which accounts for roughly 5% of Russia’s crude processing capacity, the same day.

The cumulative damage is substantial. Ukraine’s defence ministry said earlier this month that strikes had knocked out about half of Russia’s refining capacity, a figure it acknowledged could not be independently verified. Goldman Sachs estimated that Russian refinery outages are about 3 million barrels a day higher than a year ago. Moscow has restricted diesel exports for months to protect its domestic market, and Bloomberg calculations based on Vortexa data showed Russia’s seaborne fuel exports falling to about 980,000 barrels a day in the first 10 days of October before the government relaxed some of those restrictions.

Rosneft’s decision has implications beyond Russia. Global diesel supplies are already strained by the war with Iran, attacks on Middle East energy infrastructure and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. In the US, diesel prices are trading above $6 a gallon ahead of next month’s midterm elections, and the White House has tried several measures to bring them down. Those include a deal under which Russia agreed to supply diesel, starting with 300,000 metric tons and rising over the following months. Analysts noted that even the promised volumes amount to less than two weeks of US demand, and a longer outage at Rosneft’s plants makes it harder to see where the extra barrels would come from.

The slower repair approach also changes the economics of Ukraine’s campaign. Kyiv has argued that oil revenues fund most of Russia’s war effort. If Rosneft is no longer rushing to rebuild, outages are likely to last longer, and each strike is likely to have a more lasting effect. The key questions now are whether Washington renews pressure on Kyiv to halt the attacks, and how much refining capacity Russia can protect as the winter fuel season approaches.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Western Digital CEO says AI data beats compute as long-term bet after 55% revenue jump
item.description:
The after-hours drop despite a clear beat suggests positioning, not fundamentals, is driving the moment. After the stock more than doubled this year, investors appear to be taking profits in a broad retreat from AI hardware. The 28% rise in average selling price per terabyte is the key signal for storage stocks, pointing to pricing power in hard drives that could support margins across the sector if demand holds. The growing share of orders from neoclouds is a double-edged sword: it widens the customer base but links Western Digital more closely to a group facing funding strain, so credit stress among AI infrastructure providers is now a risk to watch for storage names. Thursday’s chip rout shows how quickly sentiment toward the whole AI supply chain can change, regardless of company results.

---

Earlier:

  • SK hynix drops US IPO plan for Solidigm, once eyed at up to $150 billion valuation

---

Western Digital is selling more storage at much higher prices and argues data will outlast compute as the AI opportunity, but investors locked in gains instead of buying the pitch.

Summary:

  • Western Digital’s fiscal first-quarter profit rose to $1.78 billion, or $4.63 a share, from $1.15 billion a year earlier. Adjusted earnings of $4.64 a share beat expectations of $4.11.
  • Revenue grew to $4.38 billion from $2.82 billion, ahead of the $4.14 billion forecast.
  • The blended average selling price per terabyte rose 28%, and the company says it has demand visibility to 2030 or 2031 across its top seven customers.
  • Second-quarter guidance is for adjusted earnings of $5.60 to $6.00 a share on revenue of $5.0 billion to $5.2 billion, above current estimates.
  • The quarterly dividend rises 17% to 17.5 cents a share.
  • Shares fell about 5% to 6% after hours, having already closed down 6.4% amid a broad sell-off in AI-related stocks.

--- Western Digital posted stronger-than-expected fiscal first-quarter results and guided above forecasts as demand for data storage tied to AI infrastructure drove sales volumes and prices higher. Chief Executive Irving Tan used the earnings call to argue that data, not computing power, is the more lasting AI opportunity.

The hard disk drive maker reported a profit of $1.78 billion, or $4.63 a share, up from $1.15 billion, or $3.07 a share, a year earlier. Adjusted earnings came in at $4.64 a share, comfortably ahead of the $4.11 expected by analysts polled by FactSet. Revenue rose about 55% to $4.38 billion from $2.82 billion, beating forecasts of $4.14 billion.

Pricing was a major driver. The blended average selling price per terabyte of storage rose 28% in the quarter, reflecting strong demand that allowed the company to charge more. Tan told analysts that demand is increasingly coming from customers beyond Western Digital’s traditional base, including neoclouds and frontier AI labs. He said the company now has visibility into demand to 2030 or 2031 across its top seven customers, which has strengthened its conviction that demand for hard drive storage will last.

Tan also made a broader case for the storage industry. In his view, investors focused on the computing power behind AI systems may be overlooking the data those systems produce. AI applications generate large volumes of information that must be stored and managed, he said, and storage needs will keep growing as AI adoption spreads across industries.

The argument is, of course, one a storage maker has every reason to make, and investors did not reward it on the day. Shares fell about 5.6% to around $335 after hours, having already closed down 6.4% at about $354 during a broad rotation out of AI-related stocks, sparked in part by Meta Platforms’ capital spending disclosures. Even after the fall, the stock had more than doubled this year through Thursday’s close, leaving plenty of room for profit-taking.

The company’s outlook points to further growth. For the fiscal second quarter, Western Digital expects adjusted earnings of $5.60 to $6.00 a share on revenue of $5.0 billion to $5.2 billion, well above analyst estimates of $4.84 a share and $4.57 billion. It also raised its quarterly dividend by 17% to 17.5 cents a share, payable on December 17 to shareholders of record on December 4.

The test now is whether Tan’s longer-term view holds as AI spending comes under closer scrutiny. Growing reliance on newer customers such as neoclouds broadens demand, but it also exposes Western Digital to a part of the market where funding pressures have recently intensified. That makes the durability of those orders a key issue for investors in the quarters ahead.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: SK hynix drops US IPO plan for Solidigm, once eyed at up to $150 billion valuation
item.description:
For SK Hynix shareholders, the decision removes an overhang. Investors had worried that a separate US listing would dilute the parent’s economic interest and add to the holding-company discount across a group that already includes several listed entities. That could offer some support to the shares, which have dropped about 30% since late September to near six-month lows. The move also signals that the window for large AI hardware listings has narrowed after this month’s chip sell-off and the turmoil around neocloud funding. Next week’s third-quarter results will now take focus, along with whatever funding route SK hynix chooses for Solidigm’s expansion.

----

SK Hynix has pulled the plug on Solidigm’s US float as falling chip valuations make the timing unattractive, easing a dilution worry for its own shareholders but leaving the unit’s funding question open.

Summary:

  • SK Hynix has decided not to pursue a US initial public offering of Solidigm, its US-based NAND flash and solid-state drive subsidiary.
  • The company said it ended the IPO review because of market conditions and share price trends.
  • It said Solidigm still needs investment to grow and that it will keep looking at other ways to enhance shareholder value.
  • Reports in recent weeks suggested a listing as early as 2027 that could value Solidigm at up to $150 billion and raise $10 billion to $15 billion, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley reportedly picked as lead banks.
  • SK hynix shares have fallen sharply since late September, partly on concerns that a separate listing would dilute existing shareholders.
  • SK hynix is due to report third-quarter results on October 28.

SK hynix has decided not to pursue a US initial public offering of Solidigm, its NAND flash memory and solid-state drive subsidiary, citing market conditions and share price trends.

The South Korean chipmaker said it had ended its review of a listing, but stressed that Solidigm still needs investment to grow. It added that it will continue to explore other options to enhance shareholder value. South Korea’s Korea Economic Daily first reported the decision on Friday.

The move reverses a plan that had been gathering pace. Reuters reported in late September that Solidigm was considering a US listing as early as 2027 that could value the business at up to $150 billion and raise as much as $15 billion. That would have made it the largest semiconductor IPO in the US. In early October, Bloomberg reported that Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley had been chosen to lead an offering of about $10 billion, alongside a pre-IPO funding round. SK hynix consistently said that no decision had been made and that it would weigh the potential impact on existing shareholders.

Those shareholder concerns appear to have been a key factor. Solidigm sits at the bottom of a chain of listed SK group companies, and investors worried that a separate US float would dilute SK hynix’s economic interest in the business and deepen the discount the market applies to group holding structures. SK hynix shares have fallen about 30% since the end of September to near six-month lows, as doubts about returns on AI investment, competition in memory chips and the Solidigm debate weighed on sentiment. The Seoul-listed shares fell about 5.5% on Thursday.

Market conditions have also turned less welcoming. Chip stocks suffered their steepest daily fall since June this week amid renewed concern about AI spending, while funding stress at AI infrastructure providers has made investors more selective about capital-intensive hardware stories.

Solidigm, based in Rancho Cordova, California, was formed from Intel’s NAND and SSD business, which SK hynix agreed to buy in 2020 for about $9 billion. The unit makes enterprise solid-state drives, which have been in strong demand as AI data centres expand their storage capacity.

The company’s statement leaves open how that growth will be funded. With the IPO shelved, investors will look for clues on alternatives, such as direct support from the parent or private capital, when SK hynix reports third-quarter results on October 28.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ECB preview: MUFG sees October hold, two hikes ahead. See EUR/USD year end at 1.12
item.description:
The French-German 10-year spread is the key gauge: MUFG’s scenarios put it at about 170 basis points in its base case and above 200 in a crisis, levels last associated with the euro zone debt crisis. EUR/USD has been tracking the two-year swap spread between the euro and the dollar closely, so any further scaling back of ECB hike expectations is likely to weigh on the currency, while a firm December signal would offer some support. In bonds, heavy redemptions from the ECB’s portfolio in coming months put the pace of quantitative tightening in focus. Any hint of a slowdown could ease pressure on French debt. Energy remains a swing factor: MUFG’s forecasts assume supply risks fade, so persistently high oil and gas prices tied to the Middle East conflict would challenge both its rate path and its call for a gradual euro recovery.

---

Earlier:

  • ECB’s Panetta says rising yields a drag on growth, not a crisis, ahead of rate meeting
  • BoE preview: MUFG expects November rate hike as energy shock pushes UK inflation above 4%

---

MUFG expects the ECB to hold next week as higher bond yields and French fiscal stress tighten conditions for it, but still sees two more hikes, with France the biggest risk to the euro.

Summary:

  • MUFG says the bond sell-off and French fiscal risks have removed the case for an October ECB rate hike, as officials highlight the drag from tighter financial conditions.
  • It still expects a 25 basis point hike in December and another in the first quarter of 2027, taking the policy rate to 3.00%, then a cut back to 2.75% by the third quarter of 2027.
  • Resilient activity and higher gas prices since September justify moving into slightly restrictive territory on a risk-management basis, while underlying inflation remains contained.
  • MUFG’s base case, given 45% probability, is continued French fiscal drift, with the deficit at 5.6% to 6.0% of GDP, the French-German spread near 170 basis points, and EUR/USD in a 1.08 to 1.14 range.
  • In a deeper credibility crisis (15%), it sees the spread above 200 basis points and EUR/USD between 1.02 and 1.10, with the ECB’s TPI potentially in focus.
  • MUFG forecasts EUR/USD at 1.12 by year-end, recovering gradually to 1.18 by the third quarter of 2027.

The European Central Bank is set to keep rates on hold at next week’s policy meeting, but MUFG argues the tightening cycle is not over, even as rising bond yields and French fiscal stress do some of the work for policymakers.

In its October European outlook, MUFG said the bond market sell-off and growing fiscal risks in France have taken an October rate hike off the table. ECB officials have increasingly pointed to the impact of tighter financial conditions on the outlook, and underlying inflation pressures remain contained. Even so, the bank’s strategists argue that resilient economic activity and higher gas prices since September still justify a move into slightly restrictive territory as a risk-management measure. MUFG expects a 25 basis point hike in December and another in the first quarter of 2027, taking the policy rate to 3.00%. It then sees the ECB cutting back to 2.75% by the third quarter of 2027, a path that assumes energy supply risks fade.

France is at the centre of the outlook. MUFG notes that a fragmented parliament has led successive governments to miss fiscal targets repeatedly, leaving the deficit close to 6% of GDP despite several consolidation plans. With public debt around 120% of GDP, the bank says France has little room for further slippage and is highly exposed to weaker growth or a rise in borrowing costs. The IMF’s latest forecasts already show France as the clear outlier among major European economies, with growth seen at just 0.4% this year.

The strain is visible in the bond market. The spread between French and German 10-year yields has widened to levels last seen during the euro zone debt crisis, while France’s annual interest bill has climbed to a record. MUFG suggests that a high and rising share of French debt held by foreign investors may have amplified the sell-off. Contagion has so far been limited, with Italian spreads relatively contained.

The bank sets out four scenarios ahead of France’s presidential election, in which it describes Marine Le Pen as the frontrunner. Its base case, given 45% probability, is continued drift: the government survives by relying on procedural mechanisms, measures are diluted or delayed, and the deficit stays between 5.6% and 6.0% of GDP. In that case, MUFG sees the French-German spread around 170 basis points and EUR/USD in a 1.08 to 1.14 range. It would not force an immediate ECB response, but quantitative tightening could come under review.

A deeper credibility crisis, at 15%, would bring acute political instability, a recession and a deficit well above 6% in 2027. That would push the spread above 200 basis points and drive EUR/USD down to between 1.02 and 1.10, with investors looking to the ECB’s Transmission Protection Instrument as a potential backstop. On the more positive side, limited consolidation (35%) would leave the spread near 110 basis points, while faster consolidation (5%) would narrow it to about 90 basis points and support EUR/USD in a 1.12 to 1.18 range.

For the currency, MUFG says the scaling back of ECB hike expectations has already helped weaken the euro, which has closely tracked short-term rate differentials with the US. The bank expects the dollar to remain stronger for longer. It forecasts EUR/USD at 1.12 at the end of this year before a gradual recovery to 1.14 in the first quarter of 2027, 1.16 in the second and 1.18 in the third.

With policymakers in their quiet period, next week’s statement and press conference will be watched for how much weight the ECB gives to tighter financial conditions and French fiscal risks, and whether it keeps the door open to a December move. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia flash PMI: private sector shrinks for first time in five months as prices rise
item.description:
The survey shows weaker activity alongside firmer inflation, a difficult mix for rate expectations. Falling output argues against further tightening, while faster input and output price growth argues against easing. That uncertainty could add volatility to Australian dollar and short-dated bond pricing as traders weigh the two signals. Energy is a key channel: firms cited higher energy, shipping and commodity costs, so sustained oil prices above $110 a barrel are likely to keep feeding through to Australian business costs and consumer prices. Falling business confidence also points to a risk of softer investment and hiring intentions into year-end, which equity investors in domestically focused sectors are likely to watch.

---

Earlier, looks like more rate pain ahead:

  • RBA’s Hauser puts November hike in play

---

Australia’s private sector slipped into contraction in October as higher prices and borrowing costs hit demand, yet cost pressures intensified, leaving the economy with weaker growth and firmer inflation at the same time.

Summary:

  • The S&P Global flash Australia composite PMI output index fell to 47.7 in October from 51.3, the first contraction in five months and the lowest reading since March.
  • Services activity dropped to 47.8 from 51.9, its first decline since May. The manufacturing PMI edged up to 49.7 from 49.6, and manufacturing output rose to 46.5 from 46.2, still in contraction.
  • New orders growth eased to near-neutral, with goods orders falling faster and services new business growth slowing. Export demand was broadly stable.
  • Input costs rose at the fastest pace since May, driven by energy, shipping, commodity and wage costs, and output price inflation picked up for a second month.
  • Employment rose on services hiring, and backlogs of work grew at the sharpest rate in a year and a half.
  • Business confidence stayed positive but fell to its lowest since June.

Australia’s private sector contracted in October for the first time in five months, as higher prices and rising borrowing costs weighed on demand, according to flash survey data from S&P Global. At the same time, inflation pressures intensified.

The S&P Global flash Australia composite PMI output index fell to 47.7 from 51.3 in September, dropping below the 50 level that separates growth from contraction. It was the lowest reading since March. The decline came mainly from services, where the business activity index slid to 47.8 from 51.9, the sector’s first contraction since May. Manufacturing output continued to shrink, though slightly less sharply, with its index edging up to 46.5 from 46.2. The headline manufacturing PMI was little changed at 49.7, up from 49.6.

Demand was the main source of weakness. Growth in new business slowed to near-neutral, reflecting a deeper fall in goods orders and slower growth in services. Companies in both sectors said a lack of market confidence, higher borrowing costs and broad inflationary pressures had hurt demand at the start of the fourth quarter. Overseas demand was broadly unchanged, an improvement on September’s modest decline, as manufacturers reported a smaller fall in new export orders.

Despite lower output, firms added staff in October, all of it in services. Service providers, which had cut jobs at the end of the third quarter, hired again to deal with growing workloads. Backlogs of work across the private sector rose at the fastest pace in a year and a half.

The inflation picture was less encouraging. Average input costs rose at the fastest rate since May, with manufacturers facing steeper increases than services companies. For goods producers, the rise mainly reflected supply pressures, as delivery times lengthened further. Firms in both sectors pointed to higher energy, shipping, commodity and wage costs. Companies increasingly passed those costs on to customers, lifting output price inflation for a second consecutive month.

Jingyi Pan, economics associate director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said business conditions had deteriorated at the start of the fourth quarter, with services now joining manufacturing in contraction. Based on company feedback, she attributed the downturn to higher prices and interest rates eroding demand, alongside weaker business confidence amid economic uncertainty. She warned that faster rises in both input costs and selling prices suggest inflation could stay elevated in the coming months, posing a further risk to demand in the near term.

Business sentiment remained positive overall, with firms hopeful that expansion plans would lift output over the next 12 months. However, confidence fell to its lowest level since June, as some companies cited concerns about the economic outlook and tougher operating conditions.

Final October data are due on November 2 for manufacturing and November 4 for services and the composite. Historically, flash readings have differed little from final figures.

---

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: HSBC: Gold no short-term hedge for stocks, but three forces keep long-term case intact
item.description:
Spot gold fell to under $4,040 an ounce on Thursday, its lowest since August and roughly a quarter below its January peak. The move came as the Nasdaq dropped more than 2.5%, the kind of joint sell-off HSBC describes. The main pressure on bullion runs through oil: crude (Brent) above $110 a barrel feeds inflation fears, which push up expectations of further Fed tightening and lift Treasury yields and the dollar, raising the cost of holding a metal that pays no interest. Near-term direction is likely to depend on whether equities stabilise and margin pressure eases, and on whether yields pull back from current highs. Steady central bank demand may limit the downside, but it has not been enough to reverse the trend.

---

HSBC argues gold still belongs in portfolios for the long run, but warns that when stocks fall, crowded leveraged positions turn the metal into a source of cash rather than protection.

Summary:

  • HSBC Asset Management strategists say gold’s bull run, which took prices well above $5,000 an ounce earlier this year, has stalled, with prices lower and volatility higher.
  • They say gold has failed to protect portfolios during recent stock market falls, because leveraged positions in gold are sold to meet margin calls.
  • HSBC still sees a strategic case for gold based on the debasement trade, central bank reserve diversification and geopolitical fragmentation.
  • The latest report gives no price target. In July, HSBC said gold would likely trade in a range near term, identified US yields as the main driver, and expected further gains by year-end.
  • HSBC’s chief precious metals analyst said in May that gold’s decline during the Iran conflict showed it working as a source of liquidity, not failing as a haven.
  • Spot gold fell to around $4,040 on Thursday, its lowest level since August. Its lower still as I psot now.

Gold still has a long-term role in portfolios, according to strategists at HSBC Asset Management, but investors should not rely on it to cushion short-term stock market falls. Forced selling by leveraged holders has repeatedly pulled the metal down alongside equities.

In a recent report, the strategists said gold’s strong rally, which lifted prices well above $5,000 an ounce earlier this year, has stalled, with prices falling and volatility rising. Gold has underperformed since that early-year run as soaring oil prices, rising interest rates and higher bond yields weighed on demand. Even so, they argued that the long-term case for holding gold remains intact, supported by geopolitical fragmentation and by central banks diversifying their reserves. Concerns about debt and inflation should also keep the so-called debasement trade alive, in which investors move capital into hard assets. They added that while volatility has risen, it is not extreme by historical standards.

The more pointed message concerns gold’s behaviour during equity sell-offs. Because a large amount of leveraged money has piled into gold, a sharp fall in stocks triggers margin calls, and investors sell gold to raise cash. HSBC concluded that gold may be a solid hedge against systemic risk in a multipolar world, but cannot be counted on to reduce short-term volatility. No single asset protects against every type of stress, the strategists said, which is why investors should diversify the assets they rely on for diversification.

Thursday’s trading fit that description. Spot gold fell to around $4,050 an ounce, its lowest level since August, on the same day the Nasdaq slid more than 2.5% in a broad sell-off in chip stocks.

Notably, the latest report gives no price target. That contrasts with HSBC’s more confident tone in July, when Global Chief Investment Officer Willem Sels and Global Head of Wealth Insights Lucia Ku said US Treasury yields had become the main driver of gold prices. They noted at the time that gold had not rallied during the Middle East conflict and had largely moved in line with equities. They expected the metal to stay in a range in the near term because of elevated real yields and a strong dollar, but still anticipated further gains by year-end on the back of diversification demand, central bank purchases and steady ETF inflows. With gold now about a quarter below its January peak, the absence of a target in the latest note suggests a more cautious stance.

James Steel, HSBC’s chief precious metals analyst, put a different spin on the same pattern in an interview in May. He rejected claims that gold’s fall after the strikes on Iran showed it had failed as a safe haven. As oil prices rose, inflation fears returned, bond yields and the dollar climbed and equities fell, investors needed cash, and gold provided it. In his view, the liquidation was a reaction to stress in wider financial markets: investors were cashing in an insurance policy, not abandoning it. Steel also noted that gold’s old positive link with oil had broken down, with the correlation weak and at times negative.

He pointed to structural support from Asia, where regulatory changes now allow major Chinese insurers and Indian asset managers to hold bullion. That has shifted Chinese demand towards large institutional bars and away from jewellery and coins. He said more asset managers that had never held gold are starting to add it as an alternative asset, valued because it is both a hard asset and highly liquid.

Read together, HSBC’s comments describe a market caught between two forces: long-term structural demand on one side, and short-term sensitivity to yields, the dollar and equity-driven forced selling on the other. Until Treasury yields ease or stock market volatility settles, the second force is likely to dominate.

---

item.title: JPMorgan sees hedge fund de-risking limiting stock downside, with chips the key gauge
item.description:
The JPMorgan view rests on positioning, so the key test is whether selling dries up even as headlines stay negative. A day of heavy chip losses that is not followed by more forced selling would support the argument. Momentum-driven traders such as commodity trading advisers can flip from sellers to buyers quickly once trends stabilise, which can make rebounds sharp. In credit, CoreWeave’s bonds and default-protection costs are the clearest real-time measure of neocloud funding stress, and any spread into the debt of larger technology issuers would challenge JPMorgan’s view that the problem can be contained. Higher bond yields and oil prices above $110 add a macro headwind, raising financing costs for capital-heavy AI infrastructure at the same time.

---

Earlier:

  • investingLive Americas FX news wrap 22 Oct: Nasdaq sinks as AI worries bite; Treasury yields tumble

---

JPMorgan argues the forced selling in chip stocks is largely done, but Thursday’s semiconductor rout immediately put that positioning call to the test.

Summary:

  • JPMorgan strategist Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou says the equity exposure of hedge funds has dropped far enough to suggest limited further downside for stocks.
  • His team found that hedge fund equity performance closely tracks semiconductor shares, and that tight risk limits made recent chip losses worse by forcing funds to cut positions.
  • JPMorgan sees funding concerns around neoclouds as manageable. It notes that neocloud capex of about $80 billion is small against roughly $1.8 trillion of total tech spending this year, and that the tech sector has a financing surplus of about $400 billion.
  • Information technology makes up 28% of the MSCI All Country World Index but takes 40% of hedge fund risk capital. For semiconductors, the figures are 13% and 21%.
  • The note was published Wednesday. On Thursday the Philadelphia semiconductor index fell almost 7%, its biggest daily drop since June, and the Nasdaq lost more than 2.5%.

JPMorgan believes the sell-off in global stocks may be nearing its limit, because hedge funds have already cut much of their equity exposure. However, the bank’s argument faced an immediate test when chip stocks posted their worst session in four months a day after the note was published.

In a flows and liquidity note published on Wednesday and reported by Dow Jones MarketWatch, global markets strategist Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou found a close link between the equity performance of hedge funds and semiconductor shares, as tracked by VanEck’s SMH chip ETF. The two moved closely together during the sector’s rally in the second quarter. When chips began to fall, tight risk limits forced funds to cut positions, which made the decline worse than it would otherwise have been.

The scale of that de-risking is central to JPMorgan’s view. The team believes much of the long positioning in the sector has now been unwound, including by momentum-driven investors such as commodity trading advisers, who account for a large share of daily trading. The strategists acknowledge that short-term headwinds remain, but argue that the positioning adjustment should help limit further losses.

The note also addressed concerns about neoclouds, the specialist providers that rent computing power for AI workloads. Their funding has come under scrutiny after troubles at CoreWeave and a poorly received IPO in South Korea. JPMorgan does not see those problems derailing the AI investment cycle. It argues that demand for computing power is strong enough for providers to pass higher financing costs on to customers. It also notes that neocloud capex of about $80 billion this year is small compared with roughly $1.8 trillion of total tech capex, meaning larger hyperscalers with better access to funding could absorb any shortfall. And it points out that the broader tech sector is generating about $400 billion more in cash flow than it spends on capex this year.

The strongest message in the note is about how much influence chip stocks have. Information technology accounts for 28% of the MSCI All Country World Index by market value, but 40% of the risk capital that hedge funds deploy. For semiconductors, the gap is 13% of index weight against 21% of risk capital. In JPMorgan’s view, that makes chipmakers the best single gauge of global risk appetite, because a move in the sector affects a much larger share of investor capital than its index weight suggests.

That sensitivity was clear on Thursday. The Philadelphia semiconductor index plunged nearly 7%, its biggest daily fall since late June, and the Nasdaq dropped more than 2.5%, its steepest decline since early June, according to Reuters. The trigger was a batch of AI-related earnings that renewed concern about spending. A supply warning from chip equipment maker Lam Research and a CoreWeave downgrade added to the pressure.

Not everyone shares JPMorgan’s calm on neocloud funding. Unsecured debt yields at CoreWeave have climbed to around 15%, a level usually associated with financial distress. HSBC has warned of structural concerns across the neocloud sector, while Goldman Sachs argues that CoreWeave’s reliance on asset-backed financing limits the rise in its borrowing costs.

The next few sessions should show whether Thursday’s slide was a final burst of forced selling or the start of a new leg lower. If the chips trade stabilises without further heavy de-risking, JPMorgan’s positioning call will look well timed. If funding stress spreads beyond the weakest neocloud balance sheets, the cash-flow cushion the bank highlights is likely to be tested. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ECB’s Panetta says rising yields a drag on growth, not a crisis, ahead of rate meeting
item.description:
Panetta’s remarks put the focus on sovereign spreads, especially French and Italian debt against German Bunds, as the market’s main stress gauge in the euro zone. If US yields keep rising, the spillover he describes could push periphery spreads wider, a risk for Italian bonds given his own warning. For the euro, a growth gap that favours the US alongside higher US yields is a headwind, even with the ECB still facing inflation near double its target. Oil remains the swing factor: sustained high energy prices keep inflation pressure on the ECB, while the drag from tighter financial conditions points the other way. That tension is likely to shape how markets read next week’s decision.

- With policymakers in their pre-meeting quiet period, Panetta’s warning on bond yields is a reminder that markets may already be doing some of the ECB’s tightening for it.

Summary:

  • Bank of Italy Governor Fabio Panetta said the rise in bond yields will weigh on the euro zone economy but is not critical at this stage.
  • He described the bond sell-off as global and led by the US, where growth and inflation have beaten expectations, while European growth is weaker.
  • Panetta pointed to France’s high debt and deficits as a source of pressure, said Germany’s stronger finances have limited its yield rise, and noted spillovers to Italian borrowing costs.
  • Portugal’s central bank governor Alvaro Santos Pereira called for deeper EU integration in services, transport and energy.
  • The ECB is expected to leave rates unchanged at next week’s meeting, and policymakers are in a quiet period on monetary policy.
  • Euro zone inflation is running at almost double the ECB’s 2% target because of surging energy costs.

European Central Bank Governing Council member Fabio Panetta said the recent rise in bond yields will hold back the euro zone economy, though he does not see it as critical for now. His comments come as policymakers prepare for next week’s monetary policy meeting.

Speaking in Turin on Wednesday, the Bank of Italy governor described the move in debt markets as a global phenomenon, driven over the past week by the US, where both growth and inflation have come in stronger than expected. The difficulty for Europe, he said, is that higher US rates come with firmer growth, while expansion in the euro zone is less robust. He described the result as a drag on growth rather than a crisis, according to Bloomberg.

Panetta also pointed to uneven pressure within the bloc. Germany has seen a smaller rise in yields thanks to its stronger public finances, he said, while France’s persistently high debt and budget deficits have kept attention on the bloc’s second-largest economy. He noted that sovereign debt tensions can push up borrowing costs in Italy, and that higher long-term US rates tend to spill over into European markets, including Italian financing costs.

His comments add to warnings from other ECB officials that tighter financial conditions could slow growth. A slowdown could also help contain inflation, which surging energy costs have pushed to almost double the ECB’s 2% target.

Separately on Thursday, Portugal’s central bank governor Alvaro Santos Pereira, also an ECB policymaker, called for renewed momentum behind European integration, Reuters reported. He said Europe’s difficult geopolitical environment and its technological shortcomings show the need to deepen the single market in services, transport and energy. The single market has removed many barriers, he said, but those that remain are harder to fix because they are rooted in national institutions and rules.

Neither official addressed the rate outlook directly, as ECB policymakers are in a one-week quiet period before the meeting, when they cannot comment on monetary policy. Still, the two speeches point to the same problem from different angles: Panetta to the cyclical drag from higher borrowing costs, and Santos Pereira to the structural weaknesses that limit how much growth the euro zone can generate.

That matters for the policy debate. If market-driven increases in yields are already tightening financial conditions, the case for policymakers to add to that tightening themselves becomes harder to make, at least while growth remains fragile. The ECB is widely expected to keep rates unchanged next week. Markets will watch how much weight the statement and press conference give to financial conditions, French fiscal risks and the energy-driven inflation outlook. That balance is likely to shape expectations for the meetings that follow. 

---

item.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 22 Oct: Nasdaq sinks as AI worries bite; Treasury yields tumble
item.description:
• Nasdaq sinks as chip stocks tumble
  • Mag 7 under pressure: Apple bucks the selling
  • Bitcoin follows the flows and today that flow is "risk-off" and selling.
  • The evidence mounts that the US dollar is leveraged to the AI trade
  • US treasury excels $26 billion of five-year tips at a high yield of 2.367%
  • US 10-year yields fall, near 5% level but it's for the wrong reasons
  • Crude oil buyers remain in control from a technical perspective. What would tilt the bias lower?

  • US initial jobless claims 194K vs 200K estimate. Better than expected.
  • Morning Kickstart: Stocks fall as oil rises on Iran risks
  • investingLive European session wrap: Dollar, yen and bonds kick it old school

U.S. markets traded on two tracks Thursday. Technology and AI-related shares came under renewed pressure, while the Dow and small caps managed modest gains. The Nasdaq lost 2.60%, with the more concentrated Nasdaq 100 falling 2.90%. The Dow’s near-unchanged finish did little to describe the pressure beneath the surface.

The other big move came in Treasuries, where yields plunged by roughly 15–19 basis points. That is a significant decline. Recall the 10 year note reached 5.36% just last week. It is currenly at 4.96%. 

Now, lower borrowing costs would normally give growth stocks some support. Today, that support was missing. Investors remained focused on AI spending and returns, while higher oil kept the inflation problem in the picture.

Dollar mixed; yen leads

The dollar finished mixed. It was strongest against the New Zealand dollar and weakest against the Japanese yen.

USDJPY fell 0.82% to 156.83, while USDCHF declined 0.46% to 0.8206. The sharp drop in Treasury yields helped support those moves. USDCAD also fell, down 0.21% to 1.4015, as higher oil and strong Canadian producer-price data provided a supportive backdrop for the loonie.

Elsewhere, EURUSD declined 0.17% to 1.1213, AUDUSD fell 0.14% to 0.7017, and NZDUSD dropped 0.32% to 0.5682. GBPUSD was little changed, up 0.02% at 1.3397.

The message? Selling in U.S. technology did not produce a broad rush into the dollar.

Treasury yields plunge

The late-session yield snapshot showed:

  • 2-year: 4.6524%, down 17.1 basis points.
  • 5-year: 4.7784%, down 19.2 basis points.
  • 10-year: 4.9612%, down 18.5 basis points.
  • 30-year: 5.2857%, down 15.1 basis points.

The 10-year moved below 5%, with the strongest buying concentrated in the intermediate maturities. That was consistent with investors seeking safety and reassessing the outlook for growth and monetary policy.

During the afternoon, InvestingLive reported that futures pricing assigned a 22% probability to no further Fed hike this year. That still left another increase as the more likely outcome, but traders were giving a pause more consideration. investinglive.com

U.S. stocks: Technology takes the hit

The supplied closing snapshot showed:

  • Dow industrial average: 52,873.28, +11.98 points or +0.02%.
  • S&P 500: 7,663.43, −93.74 points or −1.21%.
  • Nasdaq Composite: 26,008.86, −694.00 points or −2.60%.
  • Russell 2000: 2,784.03, +3.01 points or +0.11%.
  • Nasdaq 100: 28,958.69, −863.83 points or −2.90%.

The gap between the Nasdaq and the Dow was the story. Investors were particularly hard on the technology companies carrying much of the AI investment boom.

Meta fell around 7% during the session, with its spending plans drawing scrutiny. The concern was whether the eventual returns would justify the enormous investment. investinglive.com

My Mag 7 update highlighted Apple (closed up 1.23%) as the exception to the selling across that group. Semiconductor weakness added to the pressure on the Nasdaq indices. The Dow and Russell holding small gains showed that some money was rotating, although the negative breadth meant this was hardly a healthy session underneath. investinglive.com

Overall the Nasdaq composite had it's worst day since June 5th. The Nasdaq 100 had it's worst day since June 23. Both indices closed below their 100 day MAs. 

Economic data: Fewer layoffs, but hiring bears watching

Initial jobless claims fell to 194,000 versus 200,000 expected, with the prior week revised to 200,000 from 199,000. The four-week average declined to 197,750. Employers are still holding on to workers.

The offset came from continuing claims, which rose to 1.728 million versus 1.720 million expected. That suggests some workers are taking longer to find another job, although one weekly increase does not establish a trend.

The report offered little evidence of a sharp deterioration in employment. Nevertheless, the subsequent Treasury rally showed that the broader market’s concerns outweighed the stronger initial-claims headline.

In Canada, September producer prices rose 2.0% month over month, following 1.3%, with annual growth accelerating to 14.5%. Raw materials prices jumped 4.8% on the month and 27.0% annually.

Those are pipeline inflation pressures, rather than a direct forecast for consumer prices. Still, they complicate the Bank of Canada’s outlook after the softer CPI report earlier in the week. The supplied morning report put the probability of an October 28 hike near 80%.

Oil rises as Middle East risks persist

Crude oil was trading at $99.07, up $1.92 or approximately 1.98%.

The Middle East continued to provide support. InvestingLive’s coverage highlighted reports of preparations for possible renewed U.S.–Israeli strikes on Iran and intensifying Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Those were reported risks, rather than confirmation that another round of strikes had begun. investinglive.com

As Adam outlined in his post on the Middle East stalemate, the absence of a diplomatic breakthrough continued to hang over energy markets. investinglive.com

That leaves traders facing an uncomfortable combination: falling yields and pressure on growth shares, but oil still near $100. The bond rally does not mean the inflation risk has disappeared. 

Gold and silver fail to find support

Gold was trading at $4,021.61, down $119.41 or 2.88%. Silver fell $3.4024 or 5.87% to $54.5456.

Gold’s decline stood out because Treasury yields were sharply lower. Falling yields normally reduce the opportunity cost of holding a metal that pays no interest. Today, that relationship did not deliver support.

InvestingLive’s gold coverage discussed concerns about tighter financial conditions alongside persistent inflation risks. Position reductions and demand for cash are also plausible explanations for gold falling with equities, although the price action alone cannot establish the cause. investinglive.com

Silver’s larger decline, alongside copper falling 2.68% to $6.4030, was consistent with pressure on industrially sensitive metals as well.

Bitcoin follows the selling

Bitcoin was trading at $81,214, down $2,810 or 3.34%, in the supplied snapshot.

For this session, it followed the pressure in technology and other risk assets. The sharp decline in yields failed to attract enough buying to offset those flows. Bitcoin was offering little protection from the equity selloff.

The next session will test whether technology buyers can regain their footing and whether the Treasury rally signals growing economic concern. Friday’s U.S. flash PMIs provide another growth check, while Middle East headlines remain the wildcard for oil and inflation expectations. Lower yields gave buyers an opportunity today. In technology, gold and Bitcoin, they failed to take it.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump invokes Defense Production Act for oil as pump prices bite 12 days before midterms
item.description:
The memo does little to change the near-term oil balance, which is still driven by the Iran conflict. Brent closed around $113 on Thursday, its highest since early May, after reports that the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms. That geopolitical risk premium outweighs any supply response the Defense Production Act can deliver in the coming weeks. The measure is more relevant for refining margins and US refiners: federal financial support for capacity could, over time, ease tight diesel and gasoline cracks that have pushed pump prices above what crude alone implies. Traders are also likely to watch for further pre-election steps aimed at fuel costs, which could add headline volatility to US product futures even if their physical impact is limited.

---

With fuel costs at record seasonal highs and the midterms less than two weeks away, the White House is again using a Korean War-era law to boost oil supply, though any relief at the pump will take longer than the campaign.

Summary:

  • President Trump signed a memo determining that domestic petroleum production, refining and related activities are essential to national defense.
  • The memo invokes Section 303 of the Defense Production Act, which allows federal financial support, purchases and purchase commitments to expand capacity.
  • It builds on an April determination covering petroleum and recent steps, including a Defense Production Act-backed expansion of a Delek refinery in Texas.
  • US gasoline has topped $4 a gallon in October for the first time on record, and diesel has been above $6.
  • Fuel costs have become a central issue before the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress.
  • Brent crude closed around $113 on Thursday, its highest since May, on reports of planned renewed strikes on Iran.

US President Donald Trump has invoked Section 303 of the Defense Production Act for domestic oil, signing a memo on Thursday that determines petroleum production, refining and related activities are essential to national defense. The move is the White House’s latest attempt to tackle high fuel prices less than two weeks before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.

Section 303 lets the federal government support industrial capacity it considers vital to national defense through purchases, purchase commitments and other financial support. Full details of Thursday’s memo were not immediately available. It follows a similar determination in April covering domestic petroleum production, refining and logistics, which waived some procedural requirements and directed the Department of Energy to use those financial tools to expand capacity.

The administration has stepped up its use of the Korean War-era law in recent weeks. Vice President JD Vance announced at a campaign stop in Texas last week that the Defense Production Act would be used to expand a Delek refinery in Tyler, though neither the White House nor the company detailed the funding or the added capacity. Reuters reported earlier this month that Trump planned to direct department heads to find ways to control diesel prices before the November 3 vote, including by using the law and bypassing state and local rules that restrict energy production. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said the administration is looking to reopen as many refineries as possible.

The political pressure is clear. Gasoline averaged around $3 a gallon when Trump returned to office on a promise to lower the cost of living. Average US gasoline prices have since exceeded $4 a gallon in October for the first time on record, and diesel has traded above $6. The US Energy Information Administration put September’s average retail prices at about $4.35 for gasoline and about $6.30 for diesel, citing higher crude costs and wider refining margins. Heating oil prices in September’s consumer price data were up more than 70% from a year earlier, just as households prepare for winter.

The main driver of those costs remains the war with Iran and disruption to Gulf energy supplies. Brent crude jumped around 4% on Thursday to settle near $113 a barrel, its highest level since early May. The move followed a New York Times report that US and Israeli military planners have prepared for renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms. Trump told reporters that the US is not negotiating with Iran and that something would happen fairly soon.

That leaves the administration with limited room to bring prices down quickly. Expanding or restarting refineries takes months or longer, so the Defense Production Act measures address long-term capacity rather than the price voters will see at the pump on election day. The EIA expects retail gasoline prices to stay broadly steady in October before easing slowly in line with crude, a path that depends heavily on how the conflict with Iran develops over the coming weeks.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: OpenAI close to raising up to $30 billion at $1.25 trillion valuation, UAE investors lead
item.description:
The round gives listed markets a fresh read on how private investors are pricing frontier AI after recent volatility in AI-linked shares. A valuation below the roughly $1.4 trillion OpenAI had sought could be read as a sign of greater price discipline. That reading would matter for chipmakers such as Nvidia and for infrastructure names tied to AI capital spending. SoftBank, a major existing OpenAI investor, is among the most direct listed proxies, and its Tokyo-traded shares may respond to any new mark on the stake. The size of Gulf participation also shows how much of the AI buildout depends on sovereign capital, which ties the sector more closely to oil revenues and Middle East geopolitics.

---

Earlier:

  • Nasdaq sinks as chip stocks tumble

---

CNBC (may be gated) report. Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round.

The reported valuation is notably lower than the figure OpenAI had been seeking earlier this month. Bloomberg reported in early October that the company was looking to raise at least $30 billion at a pre-money valuation of about $1.4 trillion. According to that report, OpenAI was presenting the valuation to prospective investors as a fixed price, even though it had not yet chosen a lead investor. That approach is unusual for a private round, where investors would normally propose and negotiate terms.

Gulf money has been central to the talks from the start. Bloomberg reported that several UAE funds, including Abu Dhabi-based MGX, were discussing forming a syndicate that could contribute up to $10 billion in total, with BlackRock also in discussions to take part. MGX has backed earlier funding rounds for both OpenAI and Anthropic.

Even at $1.25 trillion, the price would mark a sharp step up from OpenAI’s last raise. The company secured about $120 billion in March at a valuation of about $850 billion, so the new pre-money figure would be nearly 50% higher than seven months ago. Adding $30 billion of new capital would put the post-money valuation at around $1.28 trillion.

Timing appears to be a factor. Reuters reported this week that OpenAI is rushing to secure commitments before Anthropic’s expected stock market listing in mid-November, since both companies draw on a similar pool of investors. Some investors see OpenAI’s push as an attempt to lock in money that might otherwise go to the Anthropic offering, according to the Reuters report. SoftBank, MGX and other existing backers were negotiating to take part. OpenAI has itself pushed back plans for an initial public offering until at least next year.

The company has been making its case to investors with revenue figures. It has told investors that annualised revenue reached about $50 billion following the launch of its GPT-6 Astra model, and that it expects to reach $70 billion by the end of the year, Reuters reported. OpenAI has also cut prices on its cheaper models, a move it says has increased usage.

The deal had not been formally announced as of the latest reports, and the terms could still change. Once the round closes, the key questions will be whether the lower valuation reflects investors pushing back on price or a deliberate trade of valuation for speed and certainty, and how much Gulf money will shape the next phase of the AI funding race. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan CPI preview: core seen at 2.1%, topping BoJ target for first time since December
item.description:
USD/JPY has held a tight range this month between just under 157 and just under 159, with the 200-day EMA just above 157.50. A firm print would test the lower end of that range, while a soft one would push the pair back toward 159, where intervention risk becomes the main defence for the yen. In JGBs, the 2-year and 5-year sectors are the most exposed to any repricing of December hike odds, with the 5-year yield near 2.3%. For the Nikkei, a stronger yen and firmer rate expectations would usually hurt exporters and help banks, but AI-linked flows are likely to matter more than the CPI unless the surprise is large. Oil remains the wildcard: sustained crude strength tied to the Middle East conflict keeps energy feeding into Japanese inflation and into the BoJ’s upcoming forecasts.

--- Japan’s core inflation is forecast to clear the BoJ’s 2% target again, which would weaken the case for patience and strengthen the case for a December hike.

Summary:

  • Japan’s national September CPI is due at 2330 GMT Thursday (7:30pm US Eastern), and core inflation (ex fresh food) is expected at 2.1% against 1.7% in August.
  • Headline inflation is seen at around 2.1% from 1.9%, and the ex fresh food and energy measure at around 2.3% from 1.9%.
  • Tokyo’s September data beat forecasts by a wide margin, with core at 2.7% and ex food and energy at 3.0%, pointing to upside risk.
  • The BoJ raised rates to 1.25% in September on a 7-2 vote and is expected to hold at its October 29-30 meeting, with December seen as the next likely move.
  • The 10-year JGB yield has eased to around 2.9% on safe-haven demand, and USD/JPY has held near 158.
  • A September trade deficit about three times the forecast continues to weigh on the yen.

Japan’s nationwide consumer inflation data for September, due at 2330 GMT on Thursday (7:30pm US Eastern), is expected to show core inflation back above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target for the first time since December. That result would strengthen the case for another rate rise before the end of the year.

Core CPI, which excludes fresh food but includes energy, is forecast to have risen 2.1% from a year earlier, according to a Reuters poll of 15 economists, up from 1.7% in August. Economists attribute much of the expected pickup to higher energy costs linked to the Middle East conflict reaching household bills. Other analysts expect headline inflation to rise to around 2.1% from 1.9%. They see the measure that excludes both fresh food and energy, often treated as a gauge of underlying price pressure, at around 2.3%, up from 1.9%.

The risk appears tilted toward a firmer reading. Tokyo’s September figures, released earlier this month, ran well ahead of forecasts: headline and core inflation both reached 2.7%, and the ex food and energy measure hit 3.0%. The Tokyo data are published about three weeks before the national numbers and are widely used as a leading indicator. The comparison is not exact, however. Part of the Tokyo jump came from the expiry of some government support measures, while nationally, electricity subsidies were still holding power prices down in August, when they were about 2.4% lower than a year earlier.

The release comes at a sensitive point for the central bank. The BoJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September, its second increase this year. The decision passed on a 7-2 vote, and the two dissenters argued that inflation was still running below target. Core inflation had stayed under 2% for seven consecutive months through August, including through both hikes. A core reading at or above consensus would weaken that objection less than a week before the October 29-30 policy meeting.

Officials have increasingly emphasised upside risks. Governor Kazuo Ueda told parliament this week that underlying inflation is very close to the 2% goal. He cited strong global demand linked to artificial intelligence alongside a tight labour market. Deputy Governor Himino has warned of the danger of acting too late. Ueda has also described the bank’s task as anchoring inflation around 2%, rather than trying to lift it as it did during the deflation era.

Even so, an October move is not the base case. Sources familiar with the bank’s thinking told Reuters that the BoJ is likely to keep rates on hold this month unless the yen weakens further and pushes up import costs. The sources said the bank is likely to raise its inflation forecast for next fiscal year as oil prices sustain price pressures for longer than expected, and to keep its focus on inflation risks, leaving room for a hike as soon as December. Market pricing assigns almost no chance to an October increase. Estimates of December odds vary by measure, from around 60% to about 80%.

Japanese government bonds have rallied ahead of the data. The 10-year yield has eased to around 2.9%, its lowest since early September, after peaking above 3.1% in late September. The 30-year yield has fallen to near 3.9%, its lowest since early August. Safe-haven demand linked to the Middle East, fiscal strains in France and volatility in AI-related equities have supported the move. Analysts at MUFG expect the 10-year to trade between 2.85% and 3.00% this week. A firm inflation print would test that rally.

The yen has been stuck. USD/JPY has spent much of October near 158, caught between expectations of further BoJ tightening and steady structural selling of the currency. Japan’s September trade deficit came in at around ¥540 billion, roughly three times the forecast, reflecting the yen that importers must sell to pay their bills. Finance Minister Katayama has not specified an intervention level, but the threat of official buying has helped limit the pair’s upside.

Equities are likely to take their direction mainly from technology. The Nikkei briefly regained the 70,000 mark earlier this month on renewed AI optimism, before a global sell-off in AI and semiconductor shares hit sentiment.

Beyond today’s data, the focus moves to next week’s BoJ quarterly outlook report. In it, the bank is expected to say that underlying inflation has roughly reached 2%, a signal of its readiness to keep raising rates. A national print that confirms the Tokyo signal would support that view. A reading below 2% would revive the dissenters’ argument and leave the yen relying more heavily on the threat of intervention. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq sinks as chip stocks tumble
item.description:
The major U.S. stock indices closed mixed, but the selling in technology shares was the dominant story. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.60%, while the Nasdaq 100 lost 2.90%. The S&P 500 also declined sharply. The Dow and Russell 2000 managed small gains, but neither offered much cushion.

Market breadth was negative. On the Nasdaq, 1,734 stocks declined versus 1,471 advancing. So although the largest losses were concentrated in technology, the weakness extended beyond a handful of heavily weighted names.

Investors continued to question whether earnings and guidance could justify expectations surrounding AI spending. Higher oil prices amid Middle East tensions added another concern. Falling Treasury yields offered little relief to technology shares during the session.

S&P 500: Buyers have repair work to do

Using the levels outlined in my earlier technical analysis, the S&P closed below its 200-hour moving average near 7,714 and its 100-hour moving average near 7,754. Those levels now become upside hurdles. Getting above and staying above them would help buyers take back some control.

Below, the rising 100-day moving average near 7,603 sits within the swing area between 7,573 and 7,617. That remains the next important support zone. Today’s close stayed above it, but a sustained break below would increase the bearish bias.

Nasdaq Composite: Below the 100-day moving average

The Nasdaq Composite closed below its 100-day moving average at 26,265.87, identified earlier today. That puts the burden on the buyers.

A recovery above that moving average—and the ability to stay above it—would ease some immediate pressure. Until then, sellers remain in control, with the September low at 25,831.74 the next downside target. Below that, attention would turn toward the 38.2% retracement at 25,036.33 and the rising 200-day moving average near 24,980.37.

The lesson for traders

A small gain in the Dow does not tell the whole market story. Breadth measures how many stocks participate, while index performance also reflects their weightings.

Today, negative breadth and sharp losses across chip and AI shares showed why traders need to look beneath the headline. For buyers, a cheaper price is only the starting point. Getting back above a broken technical level—and staying above it—is what begins to improve the trading picture.

item.title: Mag 7 under pressure: Apple bucks the selling
item.description:
Meta, Amazon and Nvidia lead the declines as AI spending concerns weigh on sentiment. The technicals help define what comes next.

The selling pressure in US stocks is intensifying, with the technology names doing much of the heavy lifting to the downside. The latest readings show:

  • Nasdaq Composite: down 2.85%.

  • Nasdaq 100: down 3.12%.

The bigger decline in the Nasdaq 100 highlights the pressure on the largest nonfinancial stocks. When the market’s heavyweight names move lower together, their size gives them considerable influence over the indices.

What is behind the selling?

The earnings news has put the cost of the AI buildout back under the microscope. Investors are questioning how much companies need to spend, how they will fund that spending, and how quickly those investments will translate into profits. Meta’s spending outlook and plans for a new class of shares have added to those concerns. Strong revenue growth alone is having a harder time satisfying the market.

Higher oil prices and continued Middle East uncertainty are adding another layer of anxiety. That combination has encouraged a move away from growth stocks, with semiconductor shares also under considerable pressure.

Six of the Mag 7 are lower. Apple is the exception.

In the supplied snapshot, the moves show:

  • Meta: down 8.01%

  • Amazon: down 5.08%

  • Nvidia: down 4.37%

  • Alphabet: down 3.56%

  • Microsoft: down 2.19%

  • Tesla: down 1.33%

  • Apple: up 0.88%

Compared with the latest index declines, Meta, Amazon, Nvidia and Alphabet are each falling more sharply than both the Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100. Microsoft and Tesla are holding up better on a relative basis, although both remain lower. Apple is the only one trading in positive territory.

So there is a clear split within the group. The selling is broad, but the intensity is different. Apple’s gain provides some support, while the larger declines elsewhere keep the pressure on the indices.

What are the technicals telling us?

The news helps explain the nervousness. The price action helps define the risk.

After moves like these, I want to know which stocks are breaking support, which are approaching their next key target, and what buyers need to reclaim to take some of the pressure off. A stock being down sharply does not, by itself, mean the selling is over.

In the video, I take a look at each of the Mag 7 stocks and the technicals telling the story. I outline the levels that keep sellers in control, where buyers could make a stand, and what would need to change to shift the bias.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin follows the flows and today that flow is "risk-off" and selling.
item.description:
The swings in bitcoin continue. The price is currently down nearly $3,000, trading near $81,000 after reaching a low of $80,836. Today’s high reached $84,294, below yesterday’s high at $84,774.

Both highs stalled ahead of the next key upside swing level at $85,578. Buyers had their shot to extend the recovery, but they could not reach that hurdle. Today, sellers have taken back control.

Bitcoin follows the risk-off flows

The move lower has been helped by risk-off sentiment across the equity markets:

  • Nasdaq Composite: Down 2.56%.

  • Nasdaq 100: Down 2.82%.

Bitcoin is following the equity market’s lead—at least today. When investors are reducing risk, bitcoin can get caught in the same selling flow. That is what the price action is showing in this session.

The lower swing area is back in play

Technically, today’s decline has taken the price into a lower swing area between $80,100 and $81,183. That area has helped define the bottom of bitcoin’s consolidation range since September 18. Monday’s low at $80,595 also stalled within that zone.

That gives traders a clear area to watch. Buyers need to defend support and push the price back above $81,183 to begin easing the immediate downside pressure. Holding support would give them a foothold, but they would still need to build on it.

For sellers, the next step is a sustained break below the lower boundary. Call $80,000 the line in the sand. Get below and stay below, and the door opens for more downside momentum.

What comes next on a break?

Below the consolidation range, the 38.2% retracement of the move higher from the July low comes in at $76,052. That becomes the next major technical target if sellers can establish control below $80,000.

The distinction is important: testing support is one thing. Breaking below it and staying below it is another. Sellers need that next shove to turn another swing within the range into a break out of the range.

In the video above, I take a look at bitcoin’s latest swings, the support being tested, and what buyers and sellers need to do next.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: The market now sees a 22% chance the Fed doesn't hike again this year
item.description:
The Fed funds futures marketr now sees a 22% that the Federal Reserve is done hiking rates for this year.

That's a big swing to where we were after the CPI report, which is the most-revelant number the Fed should be thinking about next week. Instead, the market is focused on how the FOMC will react to the stock market, which is slumping on AI capital raising fears. 

For next week's meeting, the market now sees only a 5% chance of a hike, the lowest this month. For December, it's still at a 78% chance of a hike but no longer a sure thing. January pricing is at 27 basis points, which is barely pricing in a single hike.

Looking further out the curve, the market sees 63.5 bps this year, a far cry from the 80-90 bps priced in earlier this month.

You can also see a major repricing underway in the bond market as 2-year yields are down 18 basis points to 4.64% today. It comes after Meta filed for a new class of shares. The share filingindicates that all three long-term forecasts presented to the Board contemplated raising hundreds of billions of dollars, potentially beginning as early this autumn. Management also viewed an  equity raise as “essential” to anticipated business plans and expects additional near-term capital, including equity.

The fixed income market could be taking a view that AI bonds are now tapped out and capital raising will now fall to equity. That's bad news for share prices and Meta is down 7.5% today but it could also mean less issuance of debt, which could limit crowding out in bonds. The lack of capital could also be causing jitters about the value in the broader AI build out and signal a retrechment in the entire trade.

The problem for the Fed is that a slump in AI capital raises might not be the tonic to curb inflation. The Iran blockade continues and oil prices are up $2.35 to $99.50 today with fuel prices much higher still. That will be plenty of fuel for the hawks and make for a lively debate (and maybe a split vote?) next week.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The evidence mounts that the US dollar is leveraged to the AI trade
item.description:
Today's price action is another reminder that the underpinnings of the US dollar's rally this year is AI capex spending.

It's an intense risk-off day and yet the US dollar is down on most fronts or close to flat. It just fell into negative territory against the euro on the day despite riots and debt concerns in France. It's also sitting at a one-month low against the Canadian dollar and down 120 pips against the yen.

Some of that is a sharp drop in Treasury yields but in the bigger picture, it's all one big trade: AI.

Right now, the market is questioning where all the money will come from to fund the AI build out and finding a tough time making the math work. The costs are so staggaringly high and it's so crowded that would-be lenders are tapped out and the broader investing public is skeptical of piling into a crowded trade. 

It's now abundantly clear that much of the USD outperformance in the past year has been money flowing towards the US capex buildout and associated equities. If you wanted to invest in AI, the USA was the only real game in town. Now with valuations stretched and some questions about how the frontier models will compete with open source models, the economics of it all are in question. That's leading to a reverse of the same flows that drove the USD higher.

Moreover, the fundamentals don't support the US dollar at current levels in a world that's seeing trading relationships fray and the US stuck in a quagmire in Iran. So even if AI stands still, there's a force of gravity on the US dollar that's negative and needs constant AI dollars to support it. Said differently, it's only a matter of time until the dollar retreats.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stocks are taking on water. What could steady the ships?
item.description:
The S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 are under technical pressure. Key support levels could offer a lifeline, but buyers need to prove they can hold them.

The broader US stock indices are trading near their lows for the day. If the indices were ships on the water, they would be taking on water.

Broken moving averages have tilted the technical bias toward the sellers. However, support targets loom below that could help steady the ships. The question is whether buyers can lean against those levels and force a recovery—or whether sellers punch another hole in the hull.

S&P 500: A key support zone comes into view

  • The S&P 500 has fallen below its 100-hour moving average at 7754 and 200-hour moving average at 7714. Those breaks give sellers more control and turn the moving averages into resistance on a recovery.

The next key downside focus is the rising 100-day moving average at 7603, which sits inside a swing area between 7573 and 7617.

That combination makes this an important zone for buyers. Holding it could give them a platform for a bounce. Break below 7573 and stay below, however, and the door opens for further selling momentum.

For now, support is approaching. Buyers still need to show up.

Nasdaq Composite: The broken 100-day moving average defines risk

  • The Nasdaq Composite tested its 200-hour moving average yesterday, but fell sharply at today’s open and broke below its 100-day moving average at 26265.87.

That 100-day moving average now becomes a nearby risk-defining level. Stay below it and sellers retain the technical advantage. Move back above and stay above, and some of the immediate downward pressure would ease.

Without that recovery, the next downside targets are the September low at 25831.74, followed by the 38.2% retracement at 25036.33 and the rising 200-day moving average at 24980.37.

The retracement and 200-day moving average form another important support zone. But the first job for buyers is to reclaim the broken 100-day moving average. Until then, sellers remain in control.

Nasdaq 100: Buyers get a chance against a swing area

  • The Nasdaq 100 gapped below its 100-day moving average at 29589.57 at the open and extended to a session low of 28962.36. That brought the index within about nine points of the upper boundary of a swing area between 28822 and 28953.

This is where buyers have an opportunity to make a stand.

If the index can hold that swing area, a recovery toward the broken 100-day moving average becomes a possibility. Getting back above **29589.57—and staying above—**would give buyers more control from a technical perspective.

Conversely, a break below 28822 would weaken that recovery scenario and expose the 38.2% retracement of the rally from the 2026 low at 28108.

The distinction matters: holding support can start a bounce. Reclaiming the broken moving average would strengthen the case that buyers are taking back control.

Support could steady the ships. The bias remains bearish.

The broader indices are sinking, but each has identifiable support ahead that could help slow the selling.

Support, however, is a place to watch for a response. It is not a guarantee that the decline is over. Buyers need to hold those levels and then reclaim the technical levels broken on the way down.

Until that happens, the bias remains more bearish.

In the video above, I take a look at the three broader US stock indices, the support levels that could steady the ships, and what buyers need to do to take back control.
